title: CLARITY: The Day After Tomorrow
summary: The Senate’s procedural vote to advance the CLARITY Act failed on Tuesday 49–50. The bill would have given the industry the federal market-structure framework it has sought for years.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


The Senate’s procedural vote to advance the CLARITY Act failed on Tuesday 49–50. The bill would have given the industry the federal market-structure framework it has sought for years.


-


The vote split almost entirely on party lines: every voting Dåemocrat and both independents voted no, one Democrat did not vote, and four Republicans crossed over to vote no as well. The core sticking points were ethics enforcement and stablecoin yield rules opposed by community banks, neither of which moved enough between drafts to bring holdouts on either side over the line.


-


Industry regulation now rests on a March joint interpretive release from the SEC and CFTC, which classifies 16 assets as digital commodities. That classification is an agency interpretation, not a statute, so a court could overturn it or a future commission could withdraw it.


-


Stablecoin yield appears likely to be phased out in the U.S. as OCC and FDIC rules tied to GENIUS Act implementation are expected to close the affiliate loophole that lets platforms pay rewards today, though the final rules remain subject to change.


-


Without CLARITY, banks, custodians, and broker-dealers are stuck with the status quo: no new federal registration path letting one subsidiary handle custody, trading, and settlement together, and no statutory relief from treating custodied crypto as a balance-sheet liability. Existing state-licensed players can keep operating as before, just without the efficiencies CLARITY would have created.


-


Both agencies are already moving: the CFTC is drafting a market-structure regime under existing authority, and the SEC's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal is out for comment. Neither replaces a statute, since both remain subject to Loper Bright and can be reversed by a court or a future commission without a vote in Congress.


-


The bill isn't dead technically. Tillis preserved a motion to reconsider, and a lame-duck session remains possible before the new Congress convenes. But if Democrats flip the House, the bill would need a full rewrite rather than a simple revival.


## CLARITY Act Fails: What Happened, What Are the Implications, and What Happens Next


At 3:00 p.m. on Tuesday the Senate recorded a 49–50 vote against invoking cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 3633, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. Sixty votes were required to close the discussion and push the bill forward. Forty-nine Republicans voted yes; forty-four voting Democrats and both independents voted no, four Republicans, Susan Collins (R-ME), Josh Hawley (R-MO), Jerry Moran (R-KS), and Thom Tillis (R-NC), joined the opposition, and Senator Chris Coons (D-DE) did not vote. The chamber that can take three weeks to name a post office disposed of a five-year legislative project in 42 minutes.


Republicans hold 53 seats. Going into the vote, Rand Paul (R-KY) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) were treated as long-standing no votes, which put the reliable Republican floor at 51 and meant proponents needed at least nine Democrats or independents, not seven. On the floor, Paul in fact voted yes, but three additional Republicans, Collins, Moran, and Tillis, joined Hawley in voting no. The net effect was two more Republican defections than expected, which brought the actual Republican yes total to 49 and raised the ask to eleven Democrats or independents. The seven Democrats who negotiated the bill for months (Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Mark Warner (D-VA), and Raphael Warnock (D-GA)), plus Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), who was privately urging colleagues to vote yes as late as Monday, total eight. Had every one of them voted to proceed, the count would have reached 57. The bill did not fail because Democrats withheld seven votes. It failed because the coalition was structurally short even in the best case, and the Republican defections made that visible.


**FIGURE 1**


The path to 60 did not exist even if every named Democrat had voted yes


Cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 3633, September 15, 2026. Seats, not percentages.


*Source: U.S. Senate Daily Press floor log, September 15, 2026. Tillis's (R-NC) no vote was procedural, cast to preserve the ability to move to reconsider. The best-case bar assumes all seven Democratic negotiators and Gillibrand vote yes with Republican defections unchanged.*


Two details in the record deserve more weight than they are getting. Tillis's no was cast, per the Senate floor log, specifically to preserve his standing to move to reconsider. That is a parliamentary device rather than a substantive break, and he said afterward that he would keep working to advance the bill. Coons's absence means the recorded no side would have been 51 with full attendance. Neither changes the outcome, but both bear on whether there is a coalition to revive in a lame-duck session, which we take up below. Our interpretation is that the vote revealed a floor of roughly 49 Republicans who will support market-structure legislation regardless of ethics language, a group of three to four Republicans who will not support it while the bank lobby's concerns are open, and a Democratic caucus that has now demonstrated it can hold every member on a procedural vote against a bill several of them helped write. In our view, that may warrant a reassessment of the legislative timeline.


## Four Rounds of Concessions Moved the Text but Not the Enforcement Mechanism


Republicans released four successive versions of the bill between the Banking Committee's 15–9 markup on May 14 and the floor vote: a 616-page combined text on July 22, a 630-page revision on September 10, and a 635-page "last, best, and final" offer late on September 14. We compared the last three line by line. The September 14 text made real concessions on the provision Democrats named first. The January 20, 2029 sunset, which would have terminated the ethics ban at the end of the president's term and wiped liability for conduct before then, was deleted outright. Divestiture or placement in a blind trust became mandatory rather than one of several safe harbors. The ownership threshold that triggers coverage fell from a 20% equity stake to $15,000, and the entity-revenue test fell from a majority of revenues to a plurality with a three-year lookback. The civil penalty inverted from a cap (the lesser of 10% of consideration or $500,000) to a floor (the greater of 20% or $500,000).


Republicans have a fair point: Democrats asked for ethics rules, Republicans delivered the toughest ones ever attached to a crypto bill with the president's sign-off, and Democrats still voted no. But Democrats were not objecting to how strict the rules were. They were objecting to who gets to enforce them, and that never changed. The final text let state attorneys general sue, which sounds like a real concession. In practice, for the violations that would actually reach the president, a state AG does not sue the president. The suit is filed against the U.S. Attorney General, a presidential appointee, and it runs through an unusual two-court process before anything can happen. On top of that, if a federal ethics office says an activity is allowed, no one can sue at all. And assets parked in a blind trust are shielded even if the trust itself issues or sponsors a new token. Gallego's verdict on Monday night, that the text "leaves a lot to be desired," was about this. Democrats wanted rules that someone other than the president's own appointees could enforce. Every draft from July to September kept enforcement inside the executive branch.


**FIGURE 2**


What moved, what didn't, and what it likely would have taken


Provision status across the four Senate texts, and our read on the concession that was still missing on September 15.


*Source: line-by-line comparison of Senate Legislative Counsel drafts EHF26654 (July 22), EHF26718 (September 10), and EHF26724 (September 14); Senate Banking Committee text of May 12–14. "Likely required" reflects our interpretation of senators' public statements, not a disclosed whip count.*


The last row in Figure 2 is the one most coverage has missed. On the morning of the vote, eighteen state attorneys general led by New York's Letitia James, including Republicans Kris Kobach of Kansas and Andy Wilson of Ohio, wrote to Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott (R-SC) and Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) urging a no vote unless state police powers were fully preserved. Their central legal objection was a "qualified transaction" amendment to Section 18 of the Securities Act, which they argued gives the SEC indirect preemption authority over state securities enforcement without the investor protections that normally justify preemption. That provision was identical in every draft we compared. Five of the seven Democratic negotiators (Cortez Masto, Booker, Alsobrooks, Warner, and Gallego) had their own state's attorney general on that letter. The ethics concessions were aimed at a problem Democrats named in July. The preemption problem was named in a NASAA letter in February, restated in September, and never touched. Our read is that Republicans negotiated hard on the issue that was politically visible and not at all on the one that gave five swing votes a non-Trump reason to say no.


## What the Industry Lost Is Durability, Not Access


Bitcoin fell roughly 2.9% on the day to about $75,800, while ether dropped 4.5%, XRP 9.2%, and Solana 5.4%. Public equities of crypto companies fell even more. The dispersion in that reaction is the analysis. Bitcoin has been treated as a commodity by the CFTC since 2015, trades in regulated futures, and has had spot exchange-traded products for two and a half years. Nothing about Tuesday's vote changes its legal classification or its institutional access. What CLARITY would have given bitcoin is incremental: a statutory bar on treating custodied assets as a bank balance-sheet liability, and a bank broker-dealer registration category that would have let a single regulated subsidiary custody, execute, and settle. That matters most for collateral and margining, since bitcoin at a CFTC-registered bank custodian is a cleaner asset to pledge than bitcoin at a state-licensed non-bank. It is, however, a plumbing improvement to an asset that already has plumbing.


Altcoins and intermediaries are a different story, and the equity moves say so. CLARITY's core function was to draw a durable commodity-versus-security line and create a CFTC registration regime for the exchanges, brokers, dealers, and custodians that handle assets on the commodity side of it. Without statute, that line rests on the March 17, 2026 SEC-CFTC joint interpretation, which we discuss below, and the registration regime does not exist. An exchange's regulatory perimeter, a token's listing status, and the enforceability of the developer safe harbors all remain matters of agency discretion. The industry's legislative scorecard for this Congress is still the strongest it has ever been. GENIUS is law, the House passed CLARITY 294–134 with more than seventy Democrats, and the Senate held a floor vote on market structure for the first time. But the thing on the table Tuesday was permanence, and permanence is what did not pass.


There is also a specific loss that the industry lobbied for and will now not get in any form: the criminal safe harbor. The Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (BRCA) provisions in the July and September 10 drafts shielded non-controlling developers from being treated as engaged in money transmitting. The September 14 draft removed that shield and left only civil and Bank Secrecy Act protection. Developers gave up the criminal protection to get the bill to the floor and then lost the bill. The implication is that the legal exposure of non-custodial infrastructure (validators, relayers, front-end operators) is exactly where it was before the bill, and that exposure is priced into the protocols that depend on them.


## Bitcoin Was Never the Asset Waiting on Clarity


What remains in place is more than the headlines suggest. GENIUS is fully in force and unaffected; its issuer framework, reserve requirements, and yield prohibition stand regardless of what happens to market structure. The March 17 SEC-CFTC joint interpretation continues to govern practice, classifying bitcoin and a range of other assets as digital commodities and superseding the SEC's 2019 staff framework. The SEC's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal is out for comment through October 20, and Chairman Atkins said Tuesday morning that the agency "will deliver for investors and innovators with or without the legislation." The two House committee chairmen who own market structure issued a joint statement Tuesday saying they would partner with regulators using existing authority until statute arrives. None of that is a substitute for CLARITY. But the operating environment on Wednesday morning is substantially the same as it was on Monday morning. Past market conditions, including prior price levels, are not necessarily indicative of future performance.


## The Fallback Is a 68-Page Interpretation With a Loper Bright Problem


The industry's fallback in the absence of statute is the March 17, 2026 joint SEC-CFTC interpretive release, a 68-page document that reads as a reasonable approximation of what CLARITY's classification title would have done. The problem is that it is an interpretation, and the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Loper Bright ended the Chevron deference that would once have made it durable. Courts now decide the best reading of the securities and commodities laws independently. An agency's view can inform that reading through the quality of its reasoning, but it neither binds a judge nor prevents a future commission from withdrawing it without notice-and-comment. CFTC Chairman Selig has acknowledged the exposure directly, warning that regulators could end up "writing all the rules" if Congress failed, which is a description of a stopgap rather than a substitute.


The interpretation names sixteen crypto assets as digital commodities, and the selection rule matters more than the names. The actual test is substantive: whether the asset is intrinsically linked to a functional crypto system and derives its value from that system's programmatic operation and from supply and demand, rather than from the managerial efforts of others. Each of the sixteen happens to underlie a futures contract on a CFTC-designated contract market, and the release is explicit that this is evidence rather than the rule: it names two further assets, Algorand (ALGO) and LBRY Credits (LBC), that meet the same test with no futures contract at all. That distinction matters more than it looks. A large asset with no futures market cannot assume it falls outside the framework, and a small one cannot assume a listed future is what protects it. Everything not named still has to argue its way in by analogy, with no safe harbor and no registration path either way. The practical result is a tiered market. Bitcoin sits alone at the top, with fifteen years of CFTC commodity treatment, a deep futures market, and spot ETFs that would all survive the interpretation being withdrawn. The other fifteen have the interpretation and, in some cases, futures and ETF products of their own, which is meaningfully better than nothing but is not a statute. Everything else, including Algorand and LBRY Credits, runs on the substantive test alone. Stablecoins are the exception that proves the point: GENIUS gives them an actual statute, which is why the open questions there are about yield mechanics rather than classification.


**FIGURE 3**


The digital commodities named in the March interpretation


Sixteen assets cited as examples because they underlie a CFTC futures contract, plus two, Algorand and LBRY Credits, that meet the release's substantive test with no futures contract at all.


*Source: SEC-CFTC Joint Interpretation, Release 33-11412 (March 17, 2026), pp. 13–14; law-firm summaries (Jenner & Block, Ropes & Gray, Norton Rose Fulbright). The release also names Algorand (ALGO) and LBRY Credits (LBC) as digital commodities that meet the same substantive test without underlying a CFTC futures contract. \[INSERT: market cap per asset\]*


The irony in all of this is not lost on us. The conservative legal project that produced Loper Bright was designed to constrain agencies from converting statutory ambiguity into durable policy by interpretation. It succeeded. The crypto industry is now the party most reliant on precisely that administrative flexibility, and the constraint applies to a friendly SEC and CFTC exactly as it would have applied to a hostile one. The practical exposure is twofold. A private litigant or a state regulator can challenge the March 17 framework in court and get a de novo reading of the statute, and a change in commission leadership after 2028 can withdraw it with a press release. Neither risk is imminent, but both are now priced for the full duration of whatever period passes before a statute exists, and that period just got longer.


Investors should distinguish this from the more alarmist reading that regulation by enforcement returns tomorrow. The current SEC and CFTC have no interest in that, the House has signaled active cooperation with the agencies, and the March 17 release sets a de facto standard that market participants can build against. The point is narrower: the standard is soft, and the softness is a discount that should be applied to assets and businesses whose value depends on classification, not to assets whose classification is already settled by fifteen years of agency practice and a spot ETF. That, again, is a description of altcoins and exchanges rather than bitcoin.


## The Stablecoin Yield Fight Is Being Settled by Rule, Not Statute


The second live dispute heading into Tuesday was Section 404, which would have extended GENIUS's ban on issuer-paid stablecoin yield to platforms and affiliates. GENIUS, as enacted, bars a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from paying interest or yield to holders, but it does not clearly reach an affiliate, exchange, or white-label partner that pays an economically equivalent reward through a separate entity. That is the structure under which Coinbase pays rewards on USDC issued by Circle, and Coinbase reported $1.35 billion in stablecoin revenue in 2025. The banking lobby's objection is that a reward calculated on balance and holding period is deposit interest by another name, whatever it is labeled. That objection is the reason Collins (R-ME), Moran (R-KS), and Hawley (R-MO) voted no, and the September 14 draft's 18-month Treasury circuit breaker was an attempt to buy those three votes without alienating the exchanges. It did neither.


Here we want to correct a framing that we and others used before the vote: the affiliate loophole does not "reopen" because CLARITY failed, because the agencies were already closing it on a separate track. The OCC's February 25 proposed rule implementing GENIUS creates a rebuttable presumption that coordinated arrangements between an issuer and an affiliate or related third party to pay yield are themselves prohibited, and defines "related third party" broadly enough to capture the Coinbase-Circle structure as it operates today. The FDIC's April proposal extends the same logic to bank-affiliated issuers and closes the sub-loophole where reserve interest flows to holders through a holding-company affiliate. Comment periods have closed, and final rules are expected around GENIUS's full effective date late this year. Banks, in other words, are on track to get the substance of what they wanted from Section 404 through the Comptroller's office rather than the Senate, and on a Republican-appointed Comptroller's watch.


What the industry lost on yield is therefore not the outcome but two things around it. The first is reach. OCC and FDIC rules bind banks and OCC-chartered entities cleanly, but a non-bank exchange or a DeFi lending protocol sits at the edge of their jurisdiction, and the "related third party" language becomes an interpretive fight rather than a statutory hook. Section 404 would have applied the ban to every digital asset service provider directly. The second is durability, which is the Loper Bright point again. An OCC rule can be narrowed by a court or reversed by the next Comptroller, and the exchanges still have a live shot at softening the rebuttable presumption in the final rule, in a venue with far less visibility than a floor vote. Our best guess is that yield on plain stablecoin holding inside the U.S. perimeter is ending either way, and that the interesting question for 2027 is how much of it migrates to tokenized money market funds and other explicitly regulated wrappers, which neither GENIUS nor the OCC rule addresses.


## The Lame Duck Is the Only Vehicle Left, and the Map Makes It Harder


The bill is not formally dead. Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) can refile, Tillis preserved a motion to reconsider, Senator John Kennedy (R-LA) said Tuesday it could return in the lame-duck session, and Alsobrooks said the legislation is "not going to die." A Republican Senate aide told The Block flatly that it is dead. Both statements are defensible. The text as structured has no path, and the concept survives if the enforcement mechanism moves. The lame duck is roughly four weeks between the election and the holidays, competing with appropriations, and it requires the same eleven votes that did not exist on Tuesday. Prediction markets, which had the bill near 70% after the May markup and around 17% the morning of the vote, may be a useful reference point. Whatever the odds of a lame-duck revival, they do not appear high based on currently available information, and the burden of proof has shifted to anyone arguing otherwise.


The election makes a comeback harder, not easier. Democrats are favored to take the House, where they need only three seats and the generic ballot has held near D+6 for months. The Senate is closer to a coin flip: Democrats need four seats, and forecasts range from a 59% Democratic chance at Silver Bulletin to a Republican lean elsewhere, with North Carolina, where Tillis is retiring and former Governor Roy Cooper (D) is running, as the marquee race. Either outcome is bad for a quick revival. If Democrats win the House, the bill has to be rewritten from scratch with a new majority that just watched its Senate colleagues extract concessions by voting no. If Republicans hold both chambers, the same negotiation reopens without the election-year clock, but with the same eleven-vote gap that killed it on Tuesday.


Democrats also had a simpler reason to vote no: crypto has become a liability in their own primaries. In Minnesota and Illinois this year, challengers beat sitting House members by attacking their crypto ties, and Representative Brad Sherman (D-CA) says his own polling found that hitting an opponent's crypto donations was the single best attack he had. Voters don't care much about crypto policy itself; only 4% say it affects their vote. But the industry's campaign spending is easy to turn into an attack ad, and two of the seven Democratic negotiators may run for president in 2028. For them, a yes vote in September 2026 is something an opponent can use for four years. That made every concession Republicans offered worth less than it looked.


## Implications for BitGo and Our Clients


For BitGo and our clients, the CLARITY outcome is not a setback, and our own position illustrates why. In December 2025, BitGo secured full, unconditional approval from the OCC to convert BitGo Trust Company from a South Dakota state charter into BitGo Bank & Trust, National Association, a federally chartered national trust bank. That conversion already delivers much of what CLARITY's custody provisions were designed to create by statute: a single federal supervisory regime in place of state-by-state licensing, and nationwide delivery of services where federal law preempts duplicative state requirements. The industry's broader loss on registration efficiency does not apply to us the same way; we obtained a comparable outcome through the existing OCC chartering process rather than waiting on Congress. What CLARITY would still have added is a combined custody, execution, and settlement category that our trust charter does not by itself provide. Our current assessment is that our direct exposure to classification risk is unchanged: we custody and stake many of the assets named in the March interpretation, and for assets outside that list there is no interpretation to rely on at all. To date, the current SEC and CFTC leadership have signaled a willingness to work with the industry and have begun developing their own interpretive frameworks, though the scope and durability of those efforts remain uncertain.


## Final Thoughts


The clearest signal in this note may be the one from the market. Bitcoin fell roughly 3% on news and while alts fell more, this isn’t the type of price action one might expect if years long legislation failed by a wide margin. Bitcoin is still up nearly 30% from its cycle low from a few months ago, although the past price performance is not necessarily indicative of future results and should not be relied upon as such.


One possible interpretation of recent price action is that market participants view the agency interpretation as good enough for now, and that "good enough for now" was already priced in well before Tuesday's vote. Our own framing in this note, that durability matters most for assets without bitcoin's fifteen years of agency practice, appears consistent with recent market behavior, though market conditions can change rapidly and without warning.


What we'd add is a sense of scale. This wasn't a shock repricing; it was a modest one, and it landed hardest on the assets that never had bitcoin's regulatory head start. That gap between bitcoin and everything still resting on the March 17 interpretation is, in our view, a key metric to monitor, more than any future vote count. If it holds steady or narrows, it may suggest that participants view the interpretation as sufficiently durable. If it widens as the next real test approaches, whether that test is legislative or a court case, it could signal that the regulatory uncertainty we have described is beginning to affect valuations. These are current views and are subject to change based on market, regulatory, and political developments.
